lesson.title: An If-Else That Fits on One Line
lesson.summary: Python's ternary (conditional) expression squeezes the two-outcome logic of an if-else statement into a single expression that produces a value, useful for quick assignments instead of full statement blocks.
lesson.body:
Every if-else statement covered so far chooses between two blocks of statements to run. Sometimes what you actually want is simpler: choosing between two values to use, often right inside an assignment or a function call. Writing a full if-else statement for that is not wrong, but it takes four or five lines to express something conceptually tiny. Python's ternary expression, more precisely called a conditional expression, handles exactly this case in one line: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. It is called ternary because it takes three operands: the expression to use if the condition holds, the condition itself, and the expression to use otherwise.

Compare the two forms directly. As a statement:

age = 15
if age >= 18:
    status = "adult"
else:
    status = "minor"

As a ternary expression:

age = 15
status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"

Trace the second version: Python evaluates the condition age >= 18 first. With age at 15, that is False, since 15 is less than 18. Because the condition is False, the expression evaluates to whatever follows else, which is "minor", and that value is assigned to status. Had age been 20, the condition would be True, and the expression would evaluate to "adult" instead, the value before the if. Both versions produce identical results for identical inputs; the ternary form is simply a more compact expression of the same if-else logic already introduced.

The key difference between a ternary expression and an if-else statement is not just length, it is what kind of thing each one is. An if-else statement chooses between running one block of statements or another; it does not itself produce a usable value. A ternary expression is, itself, an expression, meaning it evaluates to a single value that can be assigned, printed, passed as a function argument, or embedded inside a larger expression, such as print("Status:", "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"). You could not substitute a full if-else statement directly inside a print call like that; you would need the ternary form, or a variable set by a preceding if-else statement.

Ternary expressions are best reserved for genuinely simple choices between two values. Once either branch would require more than a short expression, or once you find yourself nesting one ternary inside another to add a third possibility, readability usually improves by switching back to a full if-else or elif statement instead. The ternary expression is a convenience for the common, simple case, not a replacement for the general-purpose conditional statement it is built from.

One more detail worth tracing carefully is evaluation order, since it reads differently from how English sentences are usually structured. Even though the condition appears in the middle of the line, Python evaluates it first, before deciding which of the two surrounding values to use, exactly as it would for a full if-else statement. Writing "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor" does not run any code speculatively for both branches, only the condition is checked up front, and then exactly one of the two value expressions is evaluated and returned, never both.
